prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My final position is a single prize part on B022 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After the first round I still rest it on the science and not on the six matching opening ballots. Holst established the human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action, Mojsov identified and synthesised the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and Drucker defined proglucagon-derived peptide biology and carried it toward therapy. Together they are one specific discovery line with a stable mechanism, confirmed in independent randomized outcome trials for glycaemia, body weight, and cardiovascular and renal endpoints. As a neuroscientist I note that the clinical consequence is demonstrated in hard outcomes and not inferred from model systems, which is the standard I apply to every candidate on the shortlist. Recognition is mature and timely.
statement.case_against: The attribution record remains the weakest point and round 1 did not settle it. Habener is outside the credited names, Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested in the public record, and Knudsen's peptide engineering, which produced the durable long-acting agonists, is left out by the three-person ceiling. I cannot verify priority dates from the supplied materials, and I do not claim to. A citation tied to physiology and the active peptide could be read as passing over the people who made the drugs work in patients. I accept that as a real cost and not a technicality. I do not think a four-name or product-centred configuration is available or better, because it would blur a discovery prize into a development prize.

responses.point: The chair argued that the UPR (B050) is the stronger second choice than optogenetics, citing its clean two-person attribution and its relevance to diabetes, neurodegeneration and secretory physiology, and asked why I placed it seventh.
responses.response: I ranked it seventh because I judged the medical consequence to be indirect and because the mammalian branches (PERK, ATF6, and the work of Ron and Kaufman) lie outside the credit to Mori and Walter. Your argument on attribution is right. The Ire1/Hac1 mechanism is original and conserved, and the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist. I also accept that optogenetics cannot be reduced to three names without leaving out a decisive contributor, so I now put B050 ahead of B034 and replace B034 with B050 among my alternatives. I still regard UPR as a basic-science prize with a conceptual, not yet therapeutic, link to disease, so it stays behind B003 for me.

responses.point: Linnarsson argued that Knudsen's exclusion is a real cost because Nobel practice rarely offers a second chance, but that the physiological framing and the three-name cap still favour Drucker, Holst and Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree with both halves. The cost is real and should be acknowledged. I do not see it as a reason to change the configuration. A two-part prize does not help because the three-person ceiling would force us to drop one of the three physiological discoverers, which would damage the core claim to make room for a development claim. I would keep the citation anchored on the physiology and the active peptide and let the words 'made possible' carry the link to the therapies, without naming the drugs. Your question about the dossier is fair. I cannot settle Mojsov's priority from what we have, but the identification and synthesis of the active form is the step that made therapeutic design possible, so I keep her in the trio.

responses.point: Perlmann would limit CAR-T (B003) to June and Sadelain, and said the missing early chimeric-receptor concept (Eshhar and others) counts against the case this year.
responses.response: I accept the two-name reading, which I already moved toward in round 1, since Rosenberg's adoptive transfer and TIL work is a separate line from CAR engineering. I agree the Eshhar gap is a real weakness, and it is the reason B003 stays an alternative and not a co-prize. I do not think it disqualifies B003, because a June and Sadelain citation worded around the design and clinical proof of CAR T cells can be fair to the earlier concept by being specific about what it credits. If the committee wanted a second part, a two-name B003 would need B022 to be cut to a single name or a pair. I do not support that trade.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius said she would not want optogenetics to compete with GLP-1 in a shared prize, because the dispute over names would dominate, and that disease-facing candidates deserve more weight.
responses.response: I agree, and this is part of why I dropped B034 from my alternatives. I ranked optogenetics third on originality and tool impact, which nobody disputes. But six credited names for three places means any triad leaves out Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenbock, and the disease link is early. That is a poor basis for a prize this year. I am not changing my view of the science. I am changing how much weight the attribution problem should carry, and your point about demonstrated disease-facing consequence supports putting B003 first among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether Habener's absence and Mojsov's contested priority make the three-person B022 configuration unfair. I cannot settle this from the supplied evidence and have not verified priority dates.
Whether the citation should name only the physiology and active peptide or signal drug development more explicitly, given that Knudsen is excluded.
Whether a June and Sadelain citation can be worded fairly to the earlier chimeric-receptor work (Eshhar and others), which determines how strong B003 is as the lead alternative.
Whether the clinical consequence of the UPR (B050) is stronger than I judge, given the chair's pointer to diabetes and neurodegeneration.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosures. My documented ties are a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, and work with Patrik Ernfors. None relates to a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. A shared institution (Karolinska Institutet) with several members is not treated as a conflict.
